prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

on a line from Szymborska My departure from the city of O.? I took no leave. I’d learned to sleep angry. On a train I was contained. The water under the bridge was just that. Shunned metaphor. It did not send waves of regret or make me reflect. It did not baptize, wash away, or cleanse. The countryside appeared like the sides of any country where rain falls and cows chew yellow flowers. The world was not too much or too much with me. I stomached it. In the photograph I only look lonely because I was alone. You cannot see the envelope on my lap or the letters lodged under sweaters in my suitcase. I carried only one bag, what I could manage in a crowd. You can imagine I held a thick book from which nothing could distract me. You can imagine my head high, eyes dry. I did not see my departure as a failure, or a fall. I’d dodged a bullet. Been reborn. You can imagine it that way. Only none of it was like that, not like that at all.

Here are three ways to polish the text, depending on the specific tone you prefer. 

### Option 1: Refined & Poetic (Recommended)
*This version retains the literary rhythm and stark, poignant tone of the original while smoothing out the transitions and elevating the phrasing.*

> Inspired by a line from Szymborska: *My departure from the city of O.?* 
> 
> I took no leave. I had learned to sleep with my anger. Aboard the train, I remained contained. The water beneath the bridge was merely water; it shunned all metaphor. It offered no waves of regret, prompted no reflection, and did not baptize, wash away, or cleanse. The passing countryside appeared much like any other land where rain falls and cows graze on yellow flowers. The world was neither too much nor too much with me—I simply stomached it. 
> 
> In the photograph, I appear lonely only because I was alone. What remains unseen is the envelope resting on my lap, or the letters tucked beneath the sweaters in my suitcase. I carried only a single bag—just what I could manage through a crowd. You might imagine me holding a thick book, utterly absorbed and undistracted. You might imagine my head held high, my eyes dry. You might assume I viewed my departure not as a failure or a fall, but as a dodged bullet—a rebirth. You can imagine it that way. 
> 
> Only none of it was like that. Not like that at all.

---

### Option 2: Professional & Narrative Prose
*This option adopts a smoother, slightly more sophisticated prose style suitable for formal essays, artistic statements, or publications.*

> Drawing from a line by Szymborska: *My departure from the city of O.?* 
> 
> I left without goodbyes, having long since learned to sleep in anger. On the train, I kept myself entirely contained. The water flowing beneath the bridge was just that—devoid of metaphor. It sent no surges of regret, invited no reflection, and offered neither baptism nor absolution. The countryside swept past like any ordinary landscape where rain falls and cattle chew yellow blossoms. The world was neither overwhelming nor intrusive; I simply endured it. 
> 
> In the photograph, I seem lonely only by virtue of being alone. Invisible to the observer are the envelope on my lap and the letters stowed under the sweaters in my luggage. I traveled light, carrying a single bag—only what I could maneuver through the throng. One could easily picture me absorbed in a heavy volume, immune to distraction, head held high and eyes clear. One could imagine I framed my departure not as a defeat or a downfall, but as a narrow escape—a moment of rebirth. It is easy to envision it that way. 
> 
> But the truth is, none of it was like that—not in the slightest.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Cadence:** Adjusted sentence boundaries to give the piece a more deliberate, resonant tempo without breaking the stream-of-consciousness feel.
* **Word Choice:** Standardized small grammatical shortcuts (e.g., changing *"I’d"* to *"I had"*, *"sides of any country"* to *"passing countryside"*) to enhance the eloquence.
* **Wordsworth Allusion:** Preserved the original line (*"The world was not too much or too much with me"*) as it is a brilliant literary reference, while polishing the sentence structure around it.

Drawing from Szymborska’s line about exiting the town of O., I quietly slipped away without saying a single farewell, having grown accustomed to going to bed while still furious. 

Boarding the railway car kept me securely enclosed. Below, the river passing beneath the trestle was purely physical, stripped of any symbolic meaning; it provoked neither remorse nor deep contemplation, nor did it offer any sort of spiritual washing, renewal, or absolution. Outside the window, the rural scenery resembled any ordinary landscape experiencing rainfall and cattle grazing on yellow blossoms. My surroundings didn't overpower me or weigh heavily on my spirit; I merely tolerated the reality around me.

Any impression of desolation in the photograph stems strictly from the physical absence of companions. Hidden from the lens are the envelope resting on my lap and the written correspondence packed beneath winter wear inside my luggage. I brought along merely a single satchel, just what I could navigate through a dense throng of people. 

An onlooker might easily picture me deeply engrossed in a heavy volume that held my undivided focus, sitting proudly upright with completely tearless eyes. It would be simple to imagine me viewing this exit not as a defeat or a downward spiral, but rather as a narrow escape from disaster or a complete fresh start. You could choose to picture the moment in those terms. 

Yet the actual reality bore zero resemblance to any of those assumptions.
outputs.L3:
Here is the expanded, fully rendered text based on your bullet points:

***

I departed from the city without ceremony, vanishing without formal goodbyes or a backward glance. My preparations were minimal; I packed only the barest necessities into a single bag, traveling as light as physically possible. Yet, what I lacked in physical luggage I made up for in emotional weight, carrying a quiet, unresolved anger that simmered just beneath the surface as the city skyline receded behind me.

As the journey unfolded, I made a conscious effort to strip the world of any poetic meaning. I actively rejected the urge to project my feelings onto the landscape or seek solace in metaphors. The barren winter trees were not symbols of grief, nor were the sprawling highways emblems of newfound freedom; they were simply wood and asphalt. I insisted on viewing the passing scenery in a strictly literal manner, using cold objectivity as a shield against my own inner turmoil. 

If an observer were to look at a photograph taken of my departure, they would see a minimalist traveler who had successfully shed their burdens. But the image conceals the true reality of the moment. Tucked away in the dark corners of that solitary bag, hidden beneath folded clothes, lay unseen letters—tangible remnants of the very conflict and personal history I was attempting to escape.

To an outsider, it is easy to romanticize such a exit as a cinematic moment—a stoic, heroic act of self-reliance and grand rebirth. But the actual experience was entirely devoid of such nobility. I was not a hero embarking on a journey of self-discovery; I was simply a bitter traveler walking away from a wreckage. The reality of the departure was far colder, quieter, and messier than any romanticized myth could ever convey.
outputs.L4:
There was no rain to wash the streets clean on the morning I left. That is the first narrative people try to impose on a departure—the poetic deluge, the ritual bath, water running down the concrete gutters carrying away the grit of accumulated years. But the sky was merely a dull, overcast gray, and the air smelled predictably of diesel exhaust and stale coffee. I did not shake the dust from my shoes in a grand, biblical gesture of leaving the past behind. I simply wiped them on the doormat so I wouldn’t track dirt into the back of the car.

We are addicted to the mythology of escape. Literature and cinema have trained us to expect a specific choreography when someone leaves a major city: the lingering, melancholy look back at the receding skyline; the dramatic soundtrack playing in the mind; the sudden, euphoric sense of catharsis as the highway opens up. We talk about leaving a city as if it were a spiritual shedding of skin, a brave, romantic purge of old ghosts and bad habits. 

I found no poetry in it. Packing a life into cardboard boxes is not a metaphor for personal transformation; it is an exhausting exercise in structural integrity, shipping tape, and deciding which cheap kitchen utensils are worth the physical space. My exit was entirely administrative. It consisted of settling a final electric bill, returning a heavy set of brass keys to a landlord who did not look up from his phone, and sitting in an unmoving bottleneck of traffic on the outbound bridge. 

In the weeks leading up to the move, friends looked at me with a quiet, reverent admiration. "It takes so much courage," they said, speaking in hushed, conspiratorial tones over drinks. "To just pull up roots and start fresh. It’s like a rebirth." They mapped their own fantasies of stoic triumph onto my exhaustion. They wanted my departure to be a heroic narrative—a bold rejection of the metropolis, a victory over the grind, a triumph of the self. They assumed I was driving away into a brighter, purer version of my life.

They were entirely wrong. 

The truth of leaving a place is far more unvarnished, far more stubborn. As the last tall building dissolved into the grey haze of the rearview mirror, there was no sudden lightness in my chest, no profound epiphany, no feeling of clean air rushing in to replace the toxic fumes of the city. My knees were cramped against the dashboard. My back ached from lifting furniture. 

The romantic vision of escape relies on the illusion that geography alters the self. But as the highway stretched into the open country, I realized the ultimate falsehood of the myth: you do not leave yourself behind in the apartment you just vacated. The city did not collapse because I left, nor did it hold its breath; it simply continued its relentless noise without me. And I did not become a new person as I crossed the state line. I was merely the same tired traveler, carrying the exact same mind, the exact same anxieties, across a slightly different arrangement of earth.
outputs.L5:
To read the poetry of Wisława Szymborska is to step into a world where the unremarked is given an audience, and the neglected is granted a voice. Throughout her work, Szymborska possessed a rare, ironic tenderness for **the shunned**—those forgotten corners of reality, the inconvenient truths, and the quiet, everyday objects that humanity steps over in its rush toward grander destinies.

Where history books record the triumphs of generals and kings, Szymborska turned her gaze to **the** bystanders, the survivors, and the mundane residue left behind when the dust of major events settles. She wrote of the abandoned dog in an empty apartment, the unloved onion weeping in its solitude, the grain of sand indifferent to being named, and **the shunned** silence that lingers after a terrible argument. 

In her famous Nobel lecture, she spoke of the value of saying "I don’t know"—a phrase often **shunned** by politicians, ideologues, and know-it-alls who demand absolute certainty. For Szymborska, however, uncertainty was the very soil in which creativity and empathy take root. She understood that **the** act of poetry is not to offer grand proclamations, but to pull **the shunned** details of life back from the brink of oblivion.

Through her light touch, sharp wit, and deep philosophical curiosity, Szymborska taught us that nothing in this universe is truly insignificant. To look at **the shunned** through her eyes is to realize that the things we ignore often hold the very secrets of what it means to be human.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem inspired by Wisława Szymborska about a quiet, un-dramatic departure from a city on a train. Have the speaker explicitly reject typical literary metaphors and romanticized views of nature, ending with a twist that subverts the narrative they just built.
counterfactuals.output:
Let the record show: no lace handkerchiefs were dabbed against weeping eyes at the platform. The stationmaster did not sound his whistle with tragic authority; he was chewing half a ham sandwich and barely looked up from his clipboard. I refuse to refer to this train as an iron serpent, a chariot of destiny, or a steel needle stitching together the fractured halves of my life. It is simply six coaches of galvanized steel, propelled by an electric motor, running nine minutes late due to a minor mechanical fault near the railyard. 

Outside, the passing birches are not bowing in silent mourning. They are birches, indifferent and green, busy converting sunlight into carbohydrates while fighting off a localized infestation of leaf miners. The sky is not gray with grief; it is gray because a cold front from the north has collided with a mass of warm, humid air over the valley. The river below the trestle bridge is not a metaphor for the relentless passage of time; it is water carrying trace amounts of agricultural runoff and a yellow plastic bucket. 

I sit in seat 42B, entirely unburdened by poetic subtext. My departure is not a dramatic ending, nor is it a grand rebirth. My chest contains no heavy stone, only a four-chambered muscle doing its routine, un-literary work. It is merely the relocation of sixty-eight kilograms of carbon, water, and bone from one zip code to another. I compliment myself on my absolute immunity to drama. I have stripped the world of its foolish pathetic fallacies. I am a rational creature moving cleanly forward into the unknown, leaving nothing behind because there was nothing monumental to leave. 

I rest my forehead against the glass—which is not cool with sorrow, merely chilled by the overhead vent—and congratulate myself on this triumph of pure logic. It is only then that the conductor punches my ticket, hands it back with a faint, sympathetic smile, and gently informs me that this is the perimeter loop, and in eleven minutes I will be delivered right back to the platform where I started.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a short piece of literary flash fiction about someone fleeing a bad relationship or situation. The narrator should sound stoic, practical, and unbothered, contrasting classic poetry tropes (like Wordsworth) with mundane reality, before revealing at the very end that their calm demeanor was a lie.
counterfactuals.output:
William Wordsworth wrote of wandering lonely as a cloud, floating high o’er vales and hills. I am currently wandering down Route 7 in a 2009 Ford Focus with a missing hubcap and a tire-pressure light that has been glowing orange since Virginia. There are no vales here. There is only a streak of endless gray asphalt, a strip mall selling discount mattresses, and the persistent smell of burnt transmission fluid.

Wordsworth would have framed Arthur’s temperament as a tempest of the soul—a tragic, brooding darkness born of poetic agony. In truth, Arthur was just a thirty-two-year-old man who threw the Roku remote at the drywall whenever his fantasy football team lost and refused to put the milk back in the fridge. When I stepped over his boots and left him sleeping at four this morning, the sky did not weep in sympathetic sorrow. It was merely damp, forty-two degrees, and smelling faintly of swamp water.

I packed with pragmatic efficiency. Three pairs of jeans, four sweaters, my grandmother’s cast-iron skillet, and the dog. A Romantic heroine would have left a scrawled note on the vanity, stained with salt tears, cursing the fickle stars. I left the spare key on the laminate counter and removed my name from the utility bills via a three-minute online portal submission. 

It is a simple matter of subtraction. Subtract his noise, add thirty miles per gallon, equal peace. 

I pull into a sun-baked rest stop outside of Scranton. A host of golden daffodils does not flutter and dance in the breeze; there is only an empty bag of Cool Ranch Doritos tumbling across the cracked pavement. I cut the engine and admire my own quietude. My breathing is shallow and deliberate. My mind is clear, unburdened by his suffocating gravity. I am entirely, remarkably unbothered. A creature of pure, clinical logic. 

I reach into the passenger seat to grab my coffee cup. 

My hand does not move. 

I tell my fingers to uncurl from the steering wheel, but they are locked to the cracked vinyl like iron brackets. I try to take another calm, measured breath, but my lungs refuse to expand, trapped behind ribs that have suddenly gone rigid. In the rearview mirror, my eyes are wide, glassy, and completely detached—even as a dry, breathless hiccup rips from my throat, and my body begins to shake so violently that the key rattles in the ignition.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue from the perspective of a traveler carrying a hidden secret (like letters in a suitcase). Use short, blunt sentences and direct address to the reader ("You can imagine..."), focusing on themes of emotional detachment and the refusal to view a departure as a tragic failure.
counterfactuals.output:
The train is late. It does not matter. I have a window seat. 

My suitcase sits between my boots. It is brown leather. Scuffed at the latch. You can imagine what is inside. You think it is wool sweaters and a spare pair of shoes. 

You are wrong. 

Under the false bottom lie forty-two letters. I did not write them. I stole them. They contain names, dates, and things that were never meant to be written down. They are heavy. Paper gets heavy when it holds the truth.

You want this to be a sad story. You want to picture me weeping on the platform. You want a tearful goodbye in the rain. 

Look at me. My eyes are dry. My hands do not shake. 

Leaving is not a tragedy. It is simple arithmetic. You subtract one person from a room. The room gets larger. That is all. 

They will wake up soon. They will find the empty drawers. They will say I failed them. They will call this a ruin. 

It is not a ruin. Failure implies that something was built to last. Nothing here was built to last. The house was already hollow. I just stopped pretending to be the furniture. 

You can imagine the guilt you think I ought to feel. Save it. Guilt is for people who plan on turning back. I bought a one-way ticket. I paid in cash. 

The letters stay with me. Not as a memory. As leverage. As proof that I was right to walk away. 

The engine turns. The floorboards vibrate beneath my soles. The town is sliding away behind the glass. It looks small. It was always small. 

Do not feel sorry for me. It is insulting. I am not running. I am just moving forward. The weight in my bag is mine, and I carry it easily.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose poem about leaving "the city of O." that wrestles with anti-metaphor. The narrator shouldn't see baptism in the water or beauty in the countryside—just plain reality—until the final line reveals the whole account might be unreliable.
counterfactuals.output:
I departed the city of O. at six in the morning, though six is merely a convention of atomic clocks and the sunrise was only the planet tilting its crust toward a medium-sized star. The exit route was asphalt—crushed limestone and bitumen laid four inches thick over compacted dirt—and it did not sigh beneath the tires. Crossing the channel, I looked down at the river. It was not a baptism. It was four million gallons of brackish water carrying industrial runoff, polystyrene fragments, and the gray, bloated belly of a dead carp. It did not wash away my youth. It did not rinse the grit from my throat; it merely obeyed a gravitational pull toward the coast. 

Past the tollgate, the countryside began. Do not ask me to call it an emerald expanse or a pastoral refuge. It was ninety acres of wet clay and invasive fescue, rutted by farm machinery and sliced by galvanized wire. The trees were not sentinels watching my flight; they were poplars and scrub oaks, dumbly competing for sunlight, their leaves turning brown because decreasing photoperiods had suppressed their chlorophyll. A crow cut across the low-stratus clouds—black not as a harbinger
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern, understated reflective text about a train ride after a fallout. Style it with dry, literary irony, referencing keeping one's head high and dodging a bullet, but end on a note of total refutation: "Only none of it was like that..."
counterfactuals.output:
The northbound commuter rail is an excellent venue for high-minded stoicism. The overhead lights are too bright, the air smells faintly of wet umbrellas, and the dark window offers a clear, flattering reflection of a person maintaining their composure against the odds.

I sat with my chin held precisely where it belonged—up, level, resolute. One has to keep one’s head high on public transit; to slouch is to invite conversation, or worse, pity from the person eating a lukewarm breakfast burrito three rows down. 

I mentally filed the evening under *necessary interventions*. In the grand narrative of my life, this was the chapter where I exercised adult restraint. I had dodged a bullet, really—a slow-moving, poorly calibrated projectile made of passive aggression and incompatible schedules, but a bullet all the same. I pictured the hypothetical future we had just erased: muted, tedious, full of polite resentment over unwashed dishes. I was out. I had saved myself hours of unproductive dialogue. I felt a quiet, intellectual pride, the kind reserved for people who cancel subscriptions before the free trial ends.

I adjusted my coat collar, stared out at the black void of the suburbs, and rehearsed the understated, dignified text I would never send. I was the cool head. I was the one who had spoken in calm, complete sentences, who had gathered their keys without a tremor, who had walked down the steps into the cool night air with the graceful finality of a foreign film protagonist. 

Only none of it was like that.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
